items.title: What the delimitation fight means and why this time is different
items.summary: Seven months after its delimitation plan was voted down, the government is trying again. Parliament reconvenes on Monday for a four-day sitting on a question India has put off for half a century: how many Lok Sabha seats each state should get. Seat shares have been frozen at 1971 population figures since 1976. That freeze lapses once the next census is published, and the government wants the terms settled before then. The April bill, the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, would have raised the Lok Sabha’s maximum strength from 543 to 850 and tied the expansion to the 33 percent reservation for women. It fell short of a two-thirds majority, 298 votes to 230 against the 352 it needed, and the government withdrew the accompanying Delimitation Bill, 2026. This time, the Union Cabinet has approved a different bill. The Constitution Bill (132nd Amendment) would write a uniform 50 percent increase in every state’s seats into the Constitution, raise the cap on the Lok Sabha to 850, and extend the freeze on each state’s share of seats to 2051. Boundaries within states would be redrawn on the latest published census, which means 2011 unless the 2027 figures are out first. Two principles are in conflict here, and both have a basis in the Constitution. One holds that every citizen’s vote should carry equal weight. The other holds that states which brought down population growth, as national policy asked, and which contribute more to the Union’s revenues, should not lose political weight as a result. items.title: Karnataka High Court introduces RFID-based case file tracking system
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has introduced an RFID-based File Tracking Module across all its registry branches to monitor the movement of case files, identify delays and improve the efficiency of file processing. In a circular dated November 24, Registrar General M Chandrashekar Reddy directed all concerned officials to strictly implement the system with effect from November 26. The initiative is part of the High Court's ongoing process of scanning and digitizing case files. RFID tags have been affixed to newly instituted cases at filing counters since June 2026. Tags are also being affixed to cases instituted before June 2026 as and when they are posted. The web-based module, developed by the High Court's engineers, links case file details with RFID tags and records the movement of files across different branches. It also enables the monitoring of the time taken by individual branches and staff members to process files and helps track their location from filing until disposal. Under the new instructions, every staff member must log into the module using their individual login credentials and scan the RFID tag of each file immediately upon receipt and before dispatch. The tag must also be scanned whenever the file is received or forwarded at subsequent stages or branches. The circular makes individual staff members responsible for ensuring that the receipt and dispatch of every file handled by them are properly recorded in the module. In case of missed scans, officials concerned must immediately inform the section officer and ensure that the necessary entry is made. Any file without an RFID tag, or technical issues involving the RFID reader, tag or tracking module, must also be reported immediately. Section Officers have been directed to regularly verify whether the receipt and dispatch of files are being properly recorded and address any missed scans, delays or other issues. They have to submit weekly compliance reports to Registrar (Judicial). [Read Circular]

items.title: Justice constrained to legal formality: Pushing citizens back to the law of Karma
items.summary: Over the course of history, the sovereign has actively assumed the responsibility of guaranteeing justice among its citizens. By doing so, the State consciously rejected the notion of justice based solely on the ‘Law of Karma', thereby discarding the ancient divine theory of justice , which assumes that a Creator or supernatural power will automatically dispense retribution and reward the righteous. By establishing structured adjudicatory mechanisms, statutory frameworks and enforcement agencies, the modern State sought to replace justice left to destiny with justice delivered by law. When procedure takes over the essence of justice On the contrary, today’s machinery of justice has become disproportionately fixated on rigid adherence to legal procedure and archaic precedents, often overlooking the actual implementation and real essence of justice. Although procedure undeniably has its own importance and is necessary to protect litigants so that their voices are not left unheard, in the rigid compliance with all these procedures, people are lost in the reach for justice. While procedural codes were enacted to ensure fairness, predictability and consistency, they have increasingly become roadblocks that trap the ordinary litigant in endless paperwork and technicalities. This ground reality goes against the long-standing principles laid down by the Supreme Court of India. In the landmark case of Sangram Singh v. Election Tribunal, Kotah (1955), Justice Vivian Bose eloquently cautioned against reducing law to hyper-technicality, observing that “our laws of procedure are grounded on a principle of natural justice which requires that men should not be condemned unheard, and that decisions should not be reached behind their backs.” Similarly, in State of Punjab v. Shamlal Murari, (1976) , Justice VR Krishna Iyer famously reminded the legal fraternity: “Processual law is not to be a tyrant but a servant, not an obstruction but an aid to justice. items.title: Karnataka High Court directs courts to accept digital copies of HC orders without insisting on physical certification
items.summary: The Karnataka High Court has directed all courts and tribunals under its administrative and supervisory control to accept digitally signed copies of its daily and final orders and not insist on physical certified copies. The directive was issued through a circular dated November 25 and came into effect on November 26. The circular states that orders and judgments downloaded in PDF format from the High Court's official website, bearing a digital signature and QR code, shall be accepted by subordinate courts and tribunals. It further clarifies that the authenticity of such orders can be verified through the digital signature, QR code or any other verification mechanism provided on the High Court's official website. “The Courts shall extend full cooperation in giving effect to the digitization initiative and shall not insist upon physical certification where the order is capable of electronic verification,” the circular states. The circular was issued by order of the Chief Justice and signed by Registrar General M Chandrashekar Reddy. The communication has been addressed to all Principal District and Sessions Judges and Unit Heads across Karnataka. [Read Circular]

items.summary: The Bombay High Court recently restored Mumbai traders’ registration of the ‘Le Shark’ trademark, a year after a single-judge ordered its removal on a rectification plea filed by UK-based company Le Shark Apparel Limited [Anil Shah Trading as Le Shark India (India) & Anr v. Le Shark Apparel Ltd & Ors] A Division Bench of Justices Bharati Dangre and Ashish S Chavan set aside the single-judge bench judgment that had allowed UK-based Le Shark Apparel's rectification plea under Sections 47 and 57 of the Trade Marks Act, 1999. The Division Bench noted that the Trade Marks Act operates territorially and does not recognise extra-territorial use of a trademark as conferring enforceable rights in India unless such use translates into legally protectable goodwill in the Indian market. The Court noted that there was not a single pleading to suggest that the UK-based company had business presence in India. "The petitioner ‘Le Shark Apparel’ has not produced on record any evidence to demonstrate its business presence in India and admittedly whatever data is furnished in the rectification application in relation to its registration, including sales, etc. is exclusively outside India," the Court found. Thus, the Court ruled that the balance of convenience clearly favoured maintaining the trademark registration in favour of the Indian traders. A single-judge in October 2025 had found fraudulent adoption by Le Shark India and a lack of genuine use in the Class 25 apparel, leading to the mark's physical removal from the register in April 2026. In appeal, the Mumbai-based company argued that the Indian registration dated back to 1991. However, the UK-based company contended that its UK predecessor created the ‘Le Shark’ name and shark graphic in 1984, built substantial global sales, and ran into the Indian mark when trying to register in India in 2015. The Division Bench ruled that the single-judge failed to consider the territorial operation of the trademark, as the UK company itself had pleaded its registration was limited to the UK. items.title: RGNUL adopts 8rney’s Agentic Legal Workspace
items.summary: The Rajiv Gandhi National University of Law, Punjab (RGNUL), has adopted 8rney , an agentic legal AI workspace, for its students, researchers and faculty members. It supports students and researchers through each stage of a project: framing a research question, finding and analysing legal materials, developing arguments, and drafting and structuring papers, dissertations and assignments. items.title: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty: Jharkhand High Court Chief Justice MS Sonak at farewell
items.summary: Judges do not deserve praise for merely doing their duty and should be willing to accept criticism, Jharkhand High Court Chief Justice Mahesh Sharadchandra Sonak said on Friday. Justice Sonak was speaking at an event held to mark his retirement from judicial service. He was elevated as an Additional Judge of the Bombay High Court in June 2013 and served there for nearly 13 years before taking over as Chief Justice of the Jharkhand High Court in January 2026. In his farewell address, he expressed his discomfort with the practice of praising judges for performing their judicial duties. "I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising the judges for doing their judicial duties. No one deserves praise for doing what he or she ought to do. Just as Oliver Wendell Holmes once bemoaned that the trouble with most of us is that we would rather be ruined by praise than be saved by criticism," said Justice Sonak. Justice MS Sonak I am not very comfortable with the general idea of praising the judges for doing their judicial duties. He went on to note that judges were not infallible. "Behind every verdict is a judge wrestling with imperfection. As judges, we are human, not infallible. As the great Benjamin Cardozo felicitously said, great tides and currents which engulf the rest of the men do not turn aside in their course and pass the judges by," said Justice Sonak. He also pointed to the pressures under which courts function. "Some of our decisions can be dialogues with generations which are yet to come. It is wrong and too great an expectation to get every judgment right. Given the pressures of our dockets we mostly decide in the heat and dust of the battlefield with no leisure for calm contemplative reflection," he noted. Justice Sonak held that criticism of judicial decisions was necessary to ensure that the judiciary remained faithful to its constitutional responsibilities. He stressed that respect for the judiciary had to be earned through its commitment to the law. "The rule of law no doubt demands reverence for the judicial office but not for the individuals who occupy it. And even that institutional respect is never an entitlement but something that must be earned and preserved each day through steadfast fidelity to law immune to the passing tides or any external noise," added Justice Sonak. items.title: DMK backs delimitation Bill, says key demands addressed
items.summary: The DMK's decision to support the revised delimitation Bill has opened up a fresh political debate in Tamil Nadu. The party, which had strongly opposed the proposed exercise over concerns that southern states could lose parliamentary representation because of their population control measures, has now announced its support for the revised proposal. However, the decision has drawn criticism from political opponents, including the ruling TVK, who accuse the DMK of abandoning its earlier opposition to delimitation. DMK leaders have defended the decision, arguing that rejecting the revised proposal could leave Tamil Nadu to a future population-based delimitation exercise following the 2027 Census and warn that the state's representation could instead fall from 39 to 31 seats.
